INTEREST OF AMICI CURIAE1
William P. Barr served twice as United States Attorney General , first under President George H.W.
Bush and mo re recently under President Donald J.
Trump. During his second tenure  as Attorney General, he declared a law enforcement emergency in rural Alaska, citing, among other concerns, alcohol
abuse and its relationship to violent crime and crimes
against children. As the Nation’s chief law enforcement officer, he also oversaw federal law enforcement
responsibilities in Indian country.
Gregg Renkes, Craig W. Richards, and Tregarrick
R. Taylor  each served as Alaska Attorney General .
Each led the department under different Alaska Governors and w as responsible for prosecuting criminal
offenses statewide and confronted the difficulties of
enforcing the law across Alaska’s vast territory, including in remote Alaska Native communities with
limited law enforcement resources.
Those experiences give amici a distinct perspective. Amici have confronted the conditions under
which crimes are investigated and prosecuted in remote communities and in jurisdictions where federal,
State, and tribal law enforcement share responsibilities. Amici submit this brief to explain why the gravity
of an offense  cannot be measured without regard to
the community  in which the conduct occurs , the
means used, or the law enforcement capacity to deter
similar conduct and prevent resulting harm.

1 No counsel for a party authored this brief in whole or in
part, and neither a party nor its counsel funded the preparation
or submission of this brief. Chenega Corporation, an Alaska Native village corporation, provided all funding for this brief.

2





INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY
In 2012, the Alaska Native village of Beaver had
84 residents and zero law enforcement officers. When
they need police help, Beaver residents must rely on
State Troopers based in Fairbanks, roughly 110 miles
away. Worse, those troopers must fly in, and response
times are (understandably) slow. Such harsh realities
prompted Beaver’s residents to address one of the biggest risks to their small community by banning  the
sale, importation, and possession of alcohol.
Petitioner Kenneth Jouppi, who operated an air -
taxi company out of Fairbanks , knew about Beaver’s
alcohol ban. Yet on the day he was arrested, one of his
planes was bound for Beaver with 72 cans of beer
aboard—nearly enough to give one can to every man,
woman, and child residing there.
Thankfully, Alaska State Troopers in Fairbanks
intercepted this bootleg shipment and seized Jouppi’s
plane. Their seizure was not happenstance. Alaska
State Troopers had been investigating Jouppi after receiving information that he had repeatedly transported passengers with alcohol to  communities that
prohibit it. Resp. Br. 13.
In Jouppi’s telling, Alaska took an airplane for a
six-pack, thus violating the Excessive Fines Clause.
But under United States v. Bajakajian, a punitive forfeiture violates the Excessive Fines Clause only if it is
“grossly disproportional to the gravity of a defendant’s
offense.” 524 U.S. 321, 334 (1998). And when calculating the gravity of an offense, context matters, abstractions do not. Six beers do not mean the same thing in
a remote, dry Alaska Native village without ready access to law enforcement as in a city where alcohol is

3





sold in grocery stores and law enforcement is minutes
away. Jouppi’s offense was grave because he was undermining the policy choices of Beaver’s residents, informed by the realities of village life, including an alcohol-related death in their small community. Gravity
must be measured in context, not  just by counting
cans.
1. Beaver’s isolation is central to the gravity of
Jouppi’s offense. Air travel is a principal means of
reaching the village, and the same geography that motivates Beaver’s alcohol ban also makes violations
hard to police. Jouppi’s own source reports that flights
into dry villages are rarely scrutinized, luggage is not
officially screened, and bootleggers commonly carry
small quantities to avoid detection.
Nor can Alaska enforce Beaver’s prohibition as
though Beaver were an ordinary municipality. Federal law and Alaska’s unusual jurisdictional history
leave the State with substantial responsibility for
criminal law enforcement in Alaska Native villages .
At the same time, immense distances, severe weather,
and sparse staffing constrain its ability to respond.
Federal officials have repeatedly recognized the result
of these circumstances : a rural Alaska public-safety
crisis. In communities where police may be hours
away, prevention and deterrence matter more.
2. Alaska is unusual, but it is not alone. Public Law
83-280, 67 Stat. 588 (1953) (“P.L. 280”) assigns certain
States a substantial criminal -enforcement role in
many tribal communities. Congress has likewise recognized that sparse policing, large geographies, and
complicated jurisdictional arrangements make criminal laws harder to enforce throughout Indian country.
Jouppi’s proposed rule would therefore reach far

4





beyond Beaver. It would systematically understate
the gravity of offenses in the communities where deterrence and prevention matter most.
3. This Court’s precedents reject Jouppi’s narrow
focus on a six -pack. Solem v. Helm directs courts assessing gravity to consider “the harm caused or
threatened to the victim or society.” 463 U.S. 277,
292–94 (1983). Harmelin v. Michigan rejected an effort to characterize an offense as victimless because
defendant’s conduct “threatened to cause grave harm
to society.” 501 U.S. 957, 1002–04 (1991) (Kennedy, J.,
concurring in part and concurring in the judgment).
And Bajakajian assessed gravity by asking what
would have happened “[h]ad [the  defendant’s] crime
gone undetected.” 524 U.S. at 339. Those cases require
consideration of a defendant’s particular conduct, the
harm it threatened, and the circumstances that gave
that threat meaning.
The means used to commit the crime matter too.
Jouppi did not merely possess prohibited alcohol
somewhere inside an airplane. His airplane was his
means of accessing an isolated village that had voted
to ban alcohol. Alaska’s Legislature treats aircraft
used for such bootlegging strictly. Federal law reflects
the same basic judgment: “[a]ny conveyance” used to
attempt to  introduce prohibited intoxicants into Indian country “shall be subject to seizure, libel, and forfeiture.” 18 U.S.C. § 3669. These judgments reflect the
commonsense principle Jouppi seeks to  erase: the
gravity of an offense turns on contextual factors, including the property used to commit the crime.
* * *

5





The question in this case is not whether six beers,
standing alone, could cause every alcohol -related
harm in rural Alaska. The question  is whether the
Constitution requires a court to pretend that Jouppi’s
six beers were headed nowhere in particular, threatened nothing, and could have been conveyed by some
other means. It does not.
ARGUMENT
I. An offense’s gravity depends on the context
of the community it threatens.
Jouppi asks the Court to calculate the gravity of
his offense  by weighing his commercial  airplane
against a six -pack and a misdemeanor. But gravity
does not turn on the defendant’s offense  in isolation;
it must include the harm it caused or threatened, and
the circumstances under which the offense occurred.
Solem v. Helm, 463 U.S. 277, 292 (1983) (to judge the
gravity of an offense courts “measur[e] the harm
caused or threatened to the victim or society”); United
States v. Bajakajian, 524 U.S. 321, 337–39 (1998) (assessing gravity by examining the circumstances of the
offense, including its relation to other illegal activity
and the source and intended use of the currency , and
the harm it caused). To accurately calculate the gravity of Jouppi’s offense, then, a court must weigh Beaver’s remote location and lack of  local law enforcement, the conditions under which Alaska must ensure
Beaver’s public safety , Beaver’s local vote in favor of
prohibiting alcohol, and how Jouppi planned to
transport bootleg alcohol into Beaver.

6





A. Beaver presents unique law enforcement
challenges.
Context starts with place. Beaver is a small Alaska
Native village on the north bank of the Yukon River,
13 miles south of the Arctic Circle and approximately
110 miles north of Fairbanks. Beaver Village Council,
Community Plan 8 (2016). The Beaver Village Council
describes its home as a “pristine wilderness setting”
within the Yukon Flats National Wildlife Refuge, surrounded by boreal forest, wetlands, and abundant
wildlife. Id. at 8–9. But that pristine setting comes
with challenges: winter temperatures can reach 70 degrees below zero, and the surrounding landscape is
marked by permafrost, sloughs, and portions of the
Yukon River that are frozen over for much of the year.
Id. at 9. Around the time of Jouppi’s offense, Beaver
had just 84 residents, more than 95  percent of whom
identified as Alaska Native. Id. at 13; Alaska Dep’t of
Env’t Conservation, Interior Alaska Subarea Contingency Plan, Resources: Part One—Community Profiles
B-12 (Change 2, Mar. 2015).
Beaver is not linked to the nearest city —Fairbanks—by road. Rather, “[p]rimary transportation
into the village is by air,” using a State-owned gravel
airstrip. Beaver Village Council, supra, at 20. Fuel,
groceries, and other supplies arrive by air cargo or,
during summer, by barge. Ibid. Beaver’s few miles of
local road s—which principally connect homes, community facilities, the airstrip, and subsistence areas—
are not paved. Id. at 20–21. This remoteness affects
ordinary life in ways that can be difficult to comprehend. As of 2016, for instance, Beaver had no grocery
store, requiring  residents to pay to have  groceries
flown in from Fairbanks. Id. at 16.

7





Geography also limits Beaver’s access to emergency services. Residents needing a doctor, hospitalization, or dental care must fly to Fairbanks or Fort
Yukon. Beaver Village Council, supra, at 22. Law enforcement faces the same obstacles . The State  of
Alaska’s community profile identifies Beaver as
served by State Troopers in Fairbanks. Alaska Dep’t
of Env’t Conservation, supra, at B-12. In 2016, Beaver
reported that its resident Village Public Safety Officer
(“VPSO”) had left in 2013 and had not been replaced.2
Beaver Village Council, supra, at 22. Residents instead rely on State Troopers in Fairbanks. As a result,
response times are often “extremely slow.” Ibid.
Beaver is not an anomaly in rural Alaska. Congress found in 2022 that “most Alaska Native villages
are located in remote areas” that “are often inaccessible by road” and “have no local law enforcement presence.” Violence Against Women Act Reauthorization
Act of 2022 (“VAWA 2022”), Pub. L. No. 117-103, div.
W, tit. VIII, § 811(a)(2), 136 Stat. 840, 904 (2022). The
Alaska Department of Public Safety thus bears “primary responsibility for law enforcement in rural
Alaska.” Id. § 811(a)(3)(A), 136 Stat. at 904.  But the
Department’s resources are limited, with about “1 to
1.4 field officers per 1,000,000 acres.” Ibid.
A recent study by the U.S. Government Accountability Office sheds light on what those numbers mean

2 VPSOs are State-certified unarmed peace officers and first
responders who serve Alaska Native communities through a program operated by the Alaska Department of Public Safety in conjunction with regional intertribal organizations, nonprofits, and
other entities. U.S. Gov’t Accountability Off.  (“GAO”), GAO-26-
107533, Tribes in Alaska: More Clarity Needed on Concurrent
Criminal Jurisdiction and Funding Opportunities 13 (2026).

8





in practice. In one Western Alaska unit alone, 60
Troopers are responsible for more than 216,000
square miles—including more than 120 Alaska Native
villages—or approximately one Trooper for every
3,601 square miles. GAO -26-107533, at 12–13. The
VPSO program supplements that force, but it too is
thinly spread: as of June 2025, 91 VPSOs served about
162 Alaska Native communities. Id. at 13. These
VPSOs generally are not trained or equipped to address felony crimes. Id. at 16.
The result is a substantial law enforcement gap.
The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Alaska
estimates that approximately one-third of Alaska Native villages lack local law enforcement personnel. Id.
at 37. For tribal leaders in remote Western Alaska ,
that lack of coverage  sometimes means waiting days
for State Troopers to respond to emergencies. Id. at
38. Alaska Department of Public Safety officials independently identified Alaska’s vast distances and severe weather  as limiting law enforcement  presence
and response times. Id. at 38–39. Compounding the
issue, many Alaska Native villages are not connected
to the road system at all, forcing residents and law enforcement to travel by plane , boat, snowmachines, or
four-wheelers. Id. at 39–40.
All these  circumstances should matter to the
Court’s gravity analysis. They are not abstractions,
and they are not background scenery. They determine
what happens when conduct creates a need for immediate police or medical intervention. In an urban setting, police, backup officers, ambulances, hospitals,
and other emergency resources may be minutes away.
In Beaver and many other Alaska Native villages, limited law enforcement  resources covering vast areas

9





can be days away , often traveling hundreds of miles
by air to provide aid. Thus, the criminal conduct that
might be common in other communities can threaten
significant injury or death in these isolated Alaska villages with limited capacity to prevent, contain, or
remedy alcohol-fueled tragedy . No gravity inquiry
concerned with the harm an offense causes or threatens can treat those realities as irrelevant.
B. The State of Alaska bears substantial
responsibility for criminal law
enforcement in Alaska Native villages.
The conditions in remote Alaska Native villages
would challenge any government. The vastness of the
State—more than twice the size of Texas —and its
many small, isolated  communities present law enforcement challenges that simply dwarf available resources. In Alaska, the  burden falls with particular
force on the State, which acts as an indispensable provider of criminal law enforcement in Alaska Native
villages. That role reflects Alaska’s unusual legal history.
In 1958, Congress brought Alaska within P ublic
Law 280, which extend s State criminal jurisdiction
into Indian country. Pub. L. No. 85 -615, 72 Stat. 545
(1958) (codified as amended at 18 U.S.C. § 1162(a)) .
But in 1971, passage of the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act (“ANCSA”) transformed Alaska’s jurisdictional landscape. ANCSA revoked every existing
Alaska reservation except the Annette Island Reserve
and authorized the transfer of approximately 44 million acres in fee to State-chartered Alaska Native corporations. Alaska v. Native Village of Venetie  Tribal
Gov’t, 522 U.S. 520, 523 –24 (1998). This Court later

10





held that lands transferred under ANCSA generally
do not qualify as Indian country. Id. at 532–34. That
holding confirmed ANCSA’s jurisdictional sea change.
In Alaska, unlike most of Indian country, primary jurisdiction ordinarily rests with the State, rather than
the federal government and tribes. Id. at 527 note 1,
532.
The practical consequences of the lack of tribal territorial jurisdiction in Alaska have been  substantial.
The President’s Commission on Law Enforcement explained that Venetie “placed an even greater responsibility on the state’s highly centralized law enforcement and criminal justice systems” and that State law
enforcement and State courts play a “key role” in protecting public safety in Alaska Native villages. President’s Comm’n on Law Enf’t & Admin. of Just., Final
Report 192–93 (2020). So while an Alaska Native village retains inherent criminal jurisdiction over Indians present in that village,3 the State enforces ordinary State criminal laws over non-Indian offenders.
This is consistent with the U.S. Department of the
Interior’s position that recent federal developments
have not created general tribal territorial jurisdiction
in Alaska.  In 1993, the Solicitor of the Interior

3  VAWA 2022 expands the jurisdiction described in 25 U.S.C.
§ 1304  by authorizing participating tribes to exercise special
criminal jurisdiction over non -Indians, but only for specified
“covered crimes” and subject to statutory limits. 25 U.S.C . §§
1304(a)(5), 1305(c) –(d). Those covered crimes include domestic
violence, sexual violence, child violence, stalking, sex trafficking,
obstruction of justice, assaults on tribal justice personnel, and
protection-order violations —not alcohol importatio n. Id. §
1304(a)(5). Congress expressly provided that VAWA does not
“limit[], alter[], expand[], or diminish[]” Alaska’s criminal jurisdiction. Id. § 1305(i)(1).

11





concluded that ANCSA had largely removed the territorial base for tribal governmental authority and that
Alaska tribes without territory generally lack authority over nonmembers absent congressional authorization. Governmental Jurisdiction of Alaska Native Villages Over Land and Nonmembers, Sol. Op. M-36975,
at 129–31 (Jan. 11, 1993). M-36975 further concluded
that there was “little or no basis” for an Alaska Native
village to assert territorial jurisdiction over an Alaska
Native allotment. Id. at 127–28. In 2024, the Solicitor
of the Interior withdrew that portion of M-36975 and
instead concluded that Alaska tribes are presumptively entitled to exercise jurisdiction over Alaska Native allotments.  Partial Withdrawal of Solicitor’s
Opinion M -36975, Governmental Jurisdiction of
Alaska Native Villages Over Land and Nonmembers,
and Clarification of Tribal Jurisdiction Over Alaska
Native Allotments, Sol. Op. M-37079, at 1 –2 (Feb. 1,
2024). In September 2025, the Deputy Secretary of the
Interior rescinded M-37079 and reinstated M -36975
“in its entirety” as “binding and authoritative.” U.S.
Dep’t of the Interior, Withdrawal of Solicitor Opinion
M-37079, at  1–2 (Sept. 25, 2025) . This r estored the
longstanding view that the federal government and
tribes generally lack criminal jurisdiction over non-Indians in Alaska villages.
Under this legal regime, Congress’s efforts to address the law enforcement  challenges in Alaska depend heavily on State participation. The unique jurisdictional landscape and limited law enforcement resources of the Bureau of Indian Affairs (“BIA”) result
largely in the absence of federal assistance to Alaska
Native villages, making it “critical for Tribes to leverage existing state law enforcement services.” GAO-26-

12





107533, at 34–35. Alaska, in turn, receives little federal funding for the public -safety and justice services
it provides to federally recognized tribes and Alaska
Native communities under its jurisdiction. Id. at 35.
And the State cannot rely on a conventional county
law enforcement network: Alaska has no elected sheriffs and no system of local jails. The Alaska Attorney
General and Alaska State Troopers thus provide comprehensive law enforcement and prosecution services
outside traditional city limits , including for both minor and major crimes in Alaska Native villages. Id. at
12–17, 36.
In sum,  Alaska Native communities remain
“largely dependent on Alaska State Troopers for public safety and law enforcement services .” GAO-26-
107533, at 37. And their reliance interests are significant: the U.S. Attorney’s Office estimates that approximately one-third of Alaska Native villages lack local
law enforcement  personnel altogether . Id. In most
cases where there is local assistance, it is in the form
of a VPSO, not a State employee or law enforcement
officer equipped and trained  to handle felony -level
crimes. GAO-26-107533, at 13, 16. The State therefore
must protect communities separated from its troopers
by immense distances, challenging geography, severe
weather, and limited transportation infrastructure.
Id. at 37–40. When a crime occurs in many Alaska Native villages, the State is expected to investigate, catch
the offenders, and prosecute violations of law, all
while providing the personnel and infrastructure necessary to protect the community.

13





C. The federal government recognizes the
public safety crisis in rural Alaska.
Both Congress and the Executive have repeatedly
recognized the serious and persistent public -safety
problem in rural Alaska.
Several statewide forums and commissions led to
Congress creating the Alaska Rural Justice and Law
Enforcement Commission, tasked with examining law
enforcement, alcohol importation and interdiction, domestic violence and child abuse, and judicial services
in rural Alaska.  Consolidated Appropriations Act,
2004, Pub. L. No. 108 -199, div. B, tit. I, §§
112(a)(2)(A), (a)(2)(B)(i)–(iv), 118 Stat. 3, 62 (2004) .
The Commission, co-chaired by Alaska Attorney General Gregg Renkes and the U.S. Attorney for the District of Alaska, Timothy Burgess, conducted 15 public
hearings in 11 locations throughout the State taking
oral and written testimony from individuals with substantial expertise and personal experience. Among its
findings, the Commission highlighted that over 95
percent of Alaska Native  crimes were linked or attributed to alcohol  or substance abuse. Alaska Rural
Just. & L. Enf’t Comm’n, Initial Report and Recommendations of the Alaska Rural Justice and Law Enforcement Commission  40, 44 –51, 54 note 102, 92
(2006). The Commission  recommended changing
State law to combat the importation of alcohol into dry
Alaska rural villages. Id. at 40, 44–51, 57–59. In 2007
and 2008, the Alaska Legislature adopted many of
these recommendations. Alaska Rural Just. & L. Enf’t
Comm’n, Report to the United States Congress and the
Alaska State Legislature 8 (2012).

14





In 2019, the United States Attorney General William P. Barr formally declared a “law enforcement
emergency in rural Alaska” under the Emergency
Federal Law Enforcement Assistance Program  and
made $6 million immediately available to Alaska to
address the needs of Alaska Native villages. U.S.
Dep’t of Just., Attorney General William P. Barr Announces Emergency Funding to Address Public Safety
Crisis in Rural Alaska  (June 28, 2019) . In doing so,
Attorney General Barr cited both Alaska’s crime rate
and “the unique circumstances of Alaska’s geographical and jurisdictional landscape.” Ibid. The law enforcement challenges facing the State and remote
Alaska Native communities were described as “complex, unique, and dire,” while residents were experiencing “extremely high rates of violence.” Ibid. The
Attorney General further explained that Alaska’s “geographic isolation contributes to law enforcement
problems not seen anywhere else in our Nation ” and
estimated that “one-third of Alaskan villages have no
local law enforcement personnel at all.” Ibid.
Alcohol is a key part of rural Alaska’s public-safety
crisis. Among DOJ’s announced priorities were reducing violent crime and sexual assault, cutting off illegal
drugs, and “[a]ddressing the problem of alcohol abuse
and its role in violent crime and crimes against children.” Ibid. The federal response thus treated alcoholrelated harm as a source of the law enforcement emergency in rural Alaska.
Congress has reached the same conclusions about
safety in rural Alaska . In VAWA 2022, Congress
found that Alaska Native women were overrepresented among victims of domestic and sexual violence.
It further found that most Alaska Native villages are

15





remote, are often inaccessible by road, and “have no
local law enforcement presence.” Pub. L. No. 117-103,
div. W, tit. VIII, § 811(a)(1)–(3), 136 Stat. at 904–05.
Congress attempted to address these issues by creating new mechanisms for intergovernmental coordination and additional tribal criminal authority.  But
the problem s have persisted. In February 2026, the
GAO reported that Alaska was among the States with
the highest crime rates from 2018 through 2023.
GAO-26-107533, at 23 & n ote 63. The disparities affecting Alaska Native communities were even more
pronounced: American Indian and Alaska Native
women accounted for nearly half of all crime victims
for whom race and gender were reported. Id. at 23–24.
And i n Western Alaska —home to roughly half of
Alaska Native communities —tribal citizens accounted for approximately 91  percent of reported felony sexual-assault victims. Ibid.
In response, t he federal government has committed substantial resources. GAO calculated that three
DOJ offices—the Office of Justice Programs, Office on
Violence Against Women, and Office of Community
Oriented Policing Services —awarded $354.5 million
in public -safety and justice grants to Alaska tribes
and tribal organizations between fiscal years 2017
and 2024. Id. at 25. Yet GAO continued to identify
high crime, limited law enforcement presence, inadequate infrastructure, and insufficient resources as significant public -safety challenges in Alaska Native
communities. Ibid. DOJ’s 2026 Alaska Pilot Program
framing paper likewise describes Alaska Native villages as presenting a “unique legal and geographic
landscape” marked by “jurisdictional complexity, limited infrastructure, and resource constraints,” and

16





recognizes that many remote communities face serious fiscal and operational limitations. U.S. Dep’t of
Just., Framing Paper: Tribal Consultation on Implementation and Evaluation of Alaska Pilot Program
Under VAWA 2022 1–2 (2026). Congress even directed
DOJ, in selecting participants for the program, to prioritize predominantly Alaska Native villages that
lack a permanent State law enforcement presence. 25
U.S.C. § 1305(d)(3)(A)(i).
These repeated federal judgments confirm the
weight the State has ascribed to the gravity of
Jouppi’s offense. The State’s concerns are not speculative about what alcohol might do in the abstract. Federal officials have declared a law enforcement emergency in rural Alaska, Congress has legislated against
the resulting public -safety conditions, and federal
agencies continue to devote substantial resources to
address the problem. Against that backdrop, the gravity of introducing bootleg alcohol into a remote Alaska
Native village cannot be measured by counting cans
of beer alone.
D. Beaver’s decision to prohibit alcohol
multiplies the gravity of Jouppi’s offense.
Jouppi’s focus on six cans of beer strips his offense
of the context that gives it meaning. Beaver’s alcohol
ban was not imposed on the community by the State.
Alaska law allows an established village, by popular
vote, to decide whether and to what extent alcohol
should be restricted. See Alaska Stat. §§ 04.11.491(b),
04.11.499(a). In 2004, Beaver voted in favor of “prohibit[ing] the sale, importation and possession of alcoholic beverages.” Alaska Div. of Elections, State-Conducted Local Election Results (July 9, 2004). Thus, the

17





restriction Jouppi violated was the community’s decision that alcohol should not be brought into Beaver.
See Jouppi v. State, 566 P.3d 943, 948 n ote 2 (Alaska
2025) (describing Alaska’s local-option regime).
Beaver’s isolation gives its decision special force.
As explained above, Beaver is not connected to Fairbanks by road and depends mostly on air transportation for emergency services and supplies. A ban on alcohol importation can thus do something that an ordinary restriction on sales cannot: materially limit the
physical availability of alcohol in the community. But
the same isolation also makes the prohibition difficult
to enforce. As Jouppi’s own source points out, flights
into dry villages “are not often scrutinized by law enforcement,” there is “no official screening of luggage,”
and “most bootleggers import only small amounts of
alcohol to remain undetected.” Kristen A. Ogilvie, Unintended Consequences of Local Alcohol Restrictions in
Rural Alaska, 17 J. Ethnicity in Substance Abuse 16,
24 (2018); see Pet. Br. 3. So it does not matter whether
Jouppi was knowingly transporting six cans of beer or
72 cans. Such small shipments are a known means of
evading alcohol restrictions in remote villages.
Beaver’s decision to ban alcohol was hardly unreasonable. Alcohol is a psychoactive , addictive  substance, and its misuse causes harms far beyond the
drinker. Alaska’s Section of Epidemiology identifies
among the acute consequences of excessive alcohol
consumption motor -vehicle crashes and other injuries, domestic abuse, sexual assault, violent crime, suicide, and fatal overdose. Alaska Dep’t of Health &
Soc. Servs., Section of Epidemiology, Health Impacts
of Alcohol Misuse in Alaska  4 (2018). It likewise describes alcohol-use disorder as a progressive condition

18





involving tolerance, a compulsive need to drink, and
an inability to stop. Ibid. Those harms have been especially severe in Alaska. The State reported that,
from 2010 through 2016, alcohol -attributable causes
killed more Alaskans than methamphetamine - and
opioid-attributable causes combined. Id. at 3, 16.
The impacts of alcohol on Alaska Natives ha ve
been “disproportionately large.” Id. at 18. From 2010
through 2016, Alaska Natives accounted for 49  percent of the State’s alcohol-attributable deaths despite
comprising just 15 percent of Alaska’s population. In
2016, their rate of alcohol -attributable mortality was
more than seven times that of non -Alaska Natives—
80.7 deaths per 100,000 persons compared with 11.4.
Id. at 3.
The same State review found that local -option
laws can reduce alcohol’s harms: it identified studies
crediting the laws with reduced injury morbidity and
mortality and improved public safety, including a
study finding significantly lower risks of serious injury from assault and motor -vehicle collisions in dry
Alaska Native villages compared to wet villages. Id.
at 21. Beaver’s decision to prohibit alcohol thus addressed documented harms of particular consequence
to similarly situated communities. But, consistent
with Jouppi’s practice of transporting passengers with
bootleg alcohol, he did not care. See Resp. Br. 13.
On the day of the offense, a customer chartered
Jouppi’s air -taxi company to fly from Fairbanks to
Beaver. Jouppi personally loaded cargo containing the
equivalent of three cases of beer onto the airplane.
Jouppi, 566 P.3d at 949 ; Pet. App. 4a–5a. These 72
cans of bootleg beer—at least six of which were plainly
visible to Jouppi —were destined for Beaver. And

19





Jouppi acted “in his professional capacity as the operator of an air taxi company and the pilot of the airplane.” Pet. App. 20a.
The jury returned a general verdict and did not determine the quantity of alcohol for which Jouppi possessed the requisite knowledge. Id. at 5a–6a. The trial
court later found him “willfully blind” to the six beers
plainly visible in a grocery bag but did not determine
his culpability for the remaining 66 beers aboard the
aircraft. Id. at 7a, 25a–26a. Nor was Jouppi’s plane
incidental. As Jouppi’s own source recognizes, small
quantities carried on flights are particularly difficult
for law enforcement to detect—to say nothing of Beaver’s residents, who have no law enforcement  presence in their community. Ogilvie, supra, at 24.
* * *
The gravity of Jouppi’s offense cannot be calculated without accounting for the Beaver community.
The law enforcement situation that led Beaver to ban
alcohol is no abstraction. A court miscalculates the
gravity of Jouppi’s offense if it focuses on  counting
cans while disregarding where those cans were
headed, why alcohol was banned there, how that ban
protects the community, and the means Jouppi used
to get around the ban . Maybe bootlegging beer by
plane is not that serious in some places, but in Beaver,
it is.

20





II. Jouppi’s narrow gravity formula would
undermine law enforcement efforts in other
tribal communities.
A. Alaska is unusual, but it is not alone.
Alaska’s jurisdictional landscape is exceptional,
but substantial State responsibility for criminal law
enforcement in many tribal communities is not. Congress passed P.L. 280 over 70 years ago in response to
what this Court has described as “the problem of lawlessness on certain Indian reservations, and the absence of adequate tribal institutions for law enforcement.” Bryan v. Itasca Cnty., 426 U.S. 373, 379 (1976).
P.L. 280’s solution was to confer on designated States
criminal jurisdiction over offenses committed by or
against Indians in Indian country  (referred to as
“mandatory P.L. 280 States”). In the areas covered by
P.L. 280, a State has jurisdiction “to the same extent”
as it does over offenses elsewhere within the State,
and its criminal laws have “the same force and effect”
there. 18 U.S.C. § 1162(a); see also California v. Cabazon Band of Mission Indians , 480 U.S. 202, 207 –08
(1987) (P.L. 280 grants States “broad criminal jurisdiction”).
Despite some changes over the years , P.L. 280 remains a major feature of Indian -country law enforcement today: the GAO recently reported that the P .L.
280 framework affects approximately 65  percent of
federally recognized tribes and that, in mandatory
P.L. 280 States, State authorities generally provide
“law enforcement, courts, and corrections” rather than
the federal government. GAO-26-107533, at 1.
P.L. 280 does not operate uniformly . Some States
historically assumed only partial jurisdiction; State

21





jurisdiction has been retroceded in some places; and
tribal criminal jurisdiction may operate concurrently
with State jurisdiction . See Washington v. Confederated Bands & Tribes of Yakima Indian Nation , 439
U.S. 463, 471–74, 498–501 (1979). Still, P.L. 280 has
resulted in State and local law enforcement agencies
playing a significant role in enforcing criminal law in
many tribal communities.  In 16 States exercising
mandatory or optional P.L. 280 jurisdiction, 93 State
prosecutors’ offices reported jurisdiction over Indian -
country felonies, and nearly three-quarters had prosecuted at least one such felony in 2007. U.S. Dep’t of
Just., Bureau of Just. Stat., State Prosecutors’ Offices
with Jurisdiction in Indian Country, 2007 , at 1 –2
(2011).
In short, P.L. 280  makes State criminal law and
State enforcement a key part of public-safety architecture in many tribal communities. And while that arrangement does not precisely replicate the State’s role
in rural Alaska, it shows that federal law has made
State officials vital in promoting public safety in many
tribal communities.
B. The practical conditions of State
enforcement in tribal communities
bear on an offense’s gravity.
Congress’s allocation of law enforcement responsibility for tribal communities to certain States is inextricably linked to the Excessive Fines Clause’s gravity
inquiry in those communities . Where federal law assigns States a substantial role in protecting tribal
communities, the practical conditions under which
that responsibility must be discharged are an inherent part of the setting in which an offense occurs.

22





Underscoring this linkage, the Tribal Law and Order Act of 2010 (“TLOA”) found that the “complicated
jurisdictional scheme” governing Indian -country
crime “has a significant negative impact on the ability
to provide public safety to Indian communities,” “has
been increasingly exploited by criminals,” and “requires a high degre e of commitment and cooperation
among tribal, Federal, and State law enforcement officials.” Pub. L. No. 111 -211, tit. II, § 202(a)(4), 124
Stat. 2258, 2262  (2010). Congress also found that
fewer than 3,000 tribal and federal law enforcement
officers patrolled more than 56 million acres of Indian
country—less than half the law enforcement presence
in comparable rural communities nationwide. Id. §
202(a)(3), 124 Stat. at 2262. Congress thus made increased coordination among federal, State, tribal, and
local law enforcement agencies an express purpose of
the Act. Id. § 202(b)(2), 124 Stat. at 2263.  On top of
that, Congress expressly authorized federal assistance for State, tribal, and local governments that enter cooperative agreements involving “mutual aid, hot
pursuit of suspects, and cross -deputization”—all to
“improv[e] law enforcement effectiveness,” “reduc [e]
crime in Indian country and nearby communities,”
and develop cooperative relationships that “effectively
combat crime.” Id. § 222, 124 Stat. at 2272.
This Court likewise has recognized that State and
tribal governments can and do share public-safety responsibilities. In McGirt v. Oklahoma , the Court observed that Oklahoma and its tribes had “proven they
can work successfully together as partners,” including
through hundreds of intergovernmental agreements
addressing law enforcement and other regulatory
matters. 591 U.S. 894, 937 (2020)  (citation omitted).

23





Those arrangements, the Court explained, reflect a
tradition of “comity and cooperative sovereignty.”
Ibid. (internal quotation marks and citation omitted).
But assigning States responsibility under P.L. 280
does not supply the States personnel and resources.
Just last year, the Senate Appropriations Committee
observed that some States with large Indian populations have “no law enforcement presence in Tribal
communities and Alaska Native Villages despite high
crime rates,” even as P.L. 280 can limit those communities’ access to certain federal public -safety funding.
S. Rep. No. 119 -46, at 69 (2025) . Congress identified
the same problem in TLOA: too few officers operating
within a “complicated jurisdictional scheme ” spanning more than 56 million acres , making criminal
laws substantially harder to enforce in Indian country. TLOA § 202(a)(3)–(4), 124 Stat. at 2262.
The Court’s proportionality cases permit those conditions to enter the excessive fines calculus . In Harmelin v. Michigan , Justice Kennedy explained that
deterrence is a legitimate penological objective and
that “differing attitudes and perceptions of local conditions may yield different, yet rational, conclusions”
about punishment for particular crimes. 501 U.S. 957,
999–1000 (1991) (Kennedy, J., concurring in part and
concurring in the judgment) . The Ninth Circuit applied the same basic principle in the excessive fines
context in Pimentel v. City of Los Angeles , 974 F.3d
917 (9th Cir. 2020). There, the court sustained a parking fine in part because the sanction had to perform a
“deterrent function” against traffic congestion “in one
of the most congested cities in the country.” Id. at 924–
25 (internal quotation marks and citation omitted) .
The offense in Pimentel was thus not assessed in a

24





vacuum. The conditions under which the law had to
operate mattered.
Here, the conditions surrounding Beaver matter.
The village has no resident law enforcement officer,
and residents rely on State Troopers in Fairbanks,
where response times can be “extremely slow.” Beaver
Village Council, supra, at 22. That makes interdiction
before bootleg alcohol reaches Beaver especially important: once it arrives, the officers responsible for enforcing the law are a plane ride away, and Alaska
must allocate scarce rural law enforcement personnel
and aircraft among competing emergencies and other
public-safety demands. The problem is compounded
because small quantities of alcohol carried on flights
are particularly difficult to detect . Ogilvie, supra, at
24. The geography, absence of local law enforcement,
and difficulty of detection are the conditions that
make deterrence especially important. No gravity inquiry can ignore this reality.
III. Jouppi miscalculates the gravity of offenses
in remote, vulnerable communities.
A. Gravity encompasses threatened harm,
not merely materialized harm.
The context in which a crime is committed is also
relevant to the gravity of an offense  because t he
Court’s proportionality cases do not limit the gravity
analysis to harm s that ha ve already materialized
when law enforcement intervenes. To the contrary,
Bajakajian derived its gross disproportionality standard from the Court’s Cruel and Unusual Punishments
Clause precedents, including Solem. Bajakajian, 524
U.S. at 336 (citing Solem, 463 U.S. at 288). Solem instructs courts assessing gravity to consider “the harm

25





caused or threatened to the victim or society,” together
with the offender’s culpability. 463 U.S. at 292–94
(emphasis added). And even those considerations are
“by no means exhaustive.” Id. at 294.
Harmelin v. Michigan illustrates this point. There,
the defendant characterized his cocaine-possession offense as nonviolent and victimless.  501 U.S. at 1002.
Justice Kennedy rejected that description because the
crime “threatened to cause grave harm to society.”
Ibid. (Kennedy, J., concurring in part and concurring
in the judgment). The gravity of the offense  in Harmelin did not turn solely on  the precise injuries the
defendant had already inflicted on an identifiable victim. It also accounted for the violence, crime, and social harms the offender’s conduct threatened. Id. at
1002–04. And those threatened harms supported
Michigan’s judgment that the offense warranted substantial punishment. Ibid.
Bajakajian employed the same type of analysis. In
concluding that the defendant’s reporting offense
caused minimal harm, the Court asked what would
have happened “[h]ad his crime gone undetected.” 524
U.S. at 339. The answer favored the defendant: “the
Government would have been deprived only of the information that $357,144 had left the country. ” Ibid.
But the Court also emphasized that the defendant’s
conduct was “unrelated to any other illegal activities”
and that he was “not a money launderer, a drug trafficker, or a tax evader.” Id. at 338. Indeed, the Court
contrasted his offense with that of “a hypothetical
drug dealer who willfully fails to report taking
$12,000 out of the country in order to purchase drugs.”
Id. at 339 . That comparison is particularly relevant
here: the Court in Bajakajian assessed gravity by

26





considering what the defendant’s particular conduct
threatened if enforcement failed. See id. at 338–39.
The principle that a gravity assessment should include threatened harm has particular force where a
law is designed to prohibit conduct before a greater
threatened harm fully materializes. When enforcement succeeds, it may limit the harm that ultimately
occurs, but  it does not erase the harm the offense
threatened. Otherwise, the same intervention that
prevents the threatened injury would artificially diminish the gravity of the offense.
The value of such preventive laws exposes another
flaw in Jouppi’s six -pack framing. Jouppi treats the
harms threatened by his  offense as  de minimis  because Alaska State Troopers intercepted the prohibited alcohol aboard his commercial aircraft before it
reached Beaver. See Jouppi, 566 P.3d at 948–49. But
the gravity inquiry should consider more: where the
alcohol was headed, what prohibition the importation
would have defeated, the harms that prohibition was
designed to prevent, the community’s capacity to prevent or contain those harms, and the means used to
introduce the alcohol.
A rule that looks only to harm realized when law
enforcement intervenes would systematically discount preventive offenses precisely when enforcement
works. Solem, Harmelin, and Bajakajian all point the
other way. And this distortion is especially serious in
communities where law enforcement  resources are
limited and distance, severe weather, and reliance on
aircraft can delay response. In those communities, deterrence necessarily carries greater weight because
the law must often prevent worse conduct before
scarce officers can be called upon to respond.

27





B. Geography and enforcement conditions
can magnify the gravity of an offense.
The threatened harm of an offense cannot be separated from the conditions in which the offense occurs.
Congress has recognized as much in addressing public
safety in tribal communities. In 2020, the Not Invisible Act, Pub. L. No. 116-166, 134 Stat. 766 (2020), directed the Secretary of the Interior to ensure that federal efforts addressing murder, trafficking, and missing Indians account for the “unique challenges of combating crime, violence, and human trafficking” faced
by tribal communities and by tribal, federal, State,
and local law enforcement. Id. § 3(a)(2), 134 Stat. at
766–67. The Act also required the Department of the
Interior to report to Congress on those efforts and recommend ways to improve federal coordination. Id. §
3(b), 134 Stat. at 767.
BIA’s 2024 Not Invisible Act report highlighted the
“unique challenges” faced by tribal communities. The
BIA explained that inadequate staffing can impair investigations, and that “[p]olicing poses unique challenges to officers in Indian Country.” U.S. Dep’t of the
Interior, Coordination of Federal Efforts to Combat
Violence Against Native People 22 (Mar. 29, 2024). On
larger reservations, “the geography of the service area
and the distant locations of support services” contribute to longer police response times. Ibid.
These challenges are nothing  new. In 1986, Congress enacted the Anti-Drug Abuse Act, which now includes provisions specifically providing targeted narcotics-enforcement assistance to the Tohono O’odham
Tribe of Arizona because its reservation lies along the
Mexican border; to the St. Regis Band of Mohawk

28





Indians of New York because its reservation lies along
the Canadian border; to the Makah Indian Tribe of
Washington because of its “proximity to international
waters”; and to the Blackfeet Nation of Montana  because its reservation also borders Canada. 25 U.S.C.
§ 2442(a)(1). Congress also directed  the Department
of the Interior to work with federal, State, tribal, and
local authorities to interdict narcotics trafficking in
Indian country. Id. § 2442(b)(1). Geography, in other
words, is not merely abstract background. Congress
has treated it as a circumstance that can alter both
the opportunity for prohibited conduct and the demands placed on law enforcement. See also Drug Enf’t
Admin., 2025 National Drug Threat Assessment  68–
69 (2025) (“remote, insular nature” of tribal communities can make it difficult for law enforcement “to investigate and respond quickly to crimes,” while the introduction and abuse of illicit substances contribute to
crime, violence, and recurring dependency).
Simply put , l ocal conditions play a role in accurately determining the harm that prohibited conduct
threatens. A remote community with limited law enforcement capacity should not be treated as though it
were a city where officers, courts, and other public -
safety resources are minutes away. Nor does considering those circumstances attribute to Jouppi abstract
societal harms untethered to his own conduct.  It
simply asks the commonsense question: What does
the defendant’s own conduct threaten in the place
where he chose to act?
All of this is why Beaver’s circumstances are relevant to gravity. Beaver is remote, law enforcement response is constrained, and the community has chosen

29





to prevent alcohol-related harms by prohibiting alcohol altogether. Those are not free-floating social problems to be laid at Jouppi’s feet. They are circumstances that bear on what the unlawful introduction
of alcohol into Beaver threatens and how readily the
resulting harm can be prevented or contained. The
Constitution does not require a court to pretend those
circumstances do not exist.
C. The means used can increase gravity.
The conditions described above also make the
means used to commit an offense relevant to its gravity. Recognizing that connection, the Alaska Legislature codified into law its judgment on how best to address the means of transportation for smuggling alcohol. Alaska law subjects aircraft, vehicles, and watercraft used to transport alcohol unlawfully into communities that prohibit its importation to forfeiture.
Alaska Stat. § 04.16.220(a)(3)(C) . But while vehicles
and watercraft are mandatorily forfeited only in specified circumstances, the statute treats aircraft differently: once an aircraft is subject to forfeiture and the
defendant is convicted, the court “shall” order its forfeiture. Id. § 04.16.220(i)–(j).
That distinction was deliberate  and should be afforded deference . See Bajakajian, 524 U.S. at  336
(“judgments about the appropriate punishment for an
offense belong in the first instance to the legislature”).
The 2004 amendments to Alaska’s bootlegging laws
were expressly presented as helping dry villages combat bootlegging. Their summary explained that dry
area protections were designed to “strengthen forfeiture law for vehicles, watercraft, and aircraft used to
bootleg alcohol.” Sectional Summary, CSSB

30





170(JUD), 23d Leg., 2d Sess. 1 ( Alaska Apr. 5, 2004).
It repeatedly described the forfeitable property as the
“means of transportation used in bootlegging.” Ibid.
Alaska thus did not treat an aircraft as fortuitously
associated with an alcohol offense : It is t he means
used to defeat a community’s alcohol prohibition that
forfeiture attempts to address.
Even so, comparison with other jurisdictions confirms that Alaska’s approach is hardly extraordinary.
See Solem, 463 U.S. at 291–92 (“courts may find it useful to compare the sentences imposed for commission
of the same crime in other jurisdictions”). Federal law
provides that “[a]ny conveyance” used to introduce or
attempt to introduce intoxicants into Indian country
where introduction is prohibited “shall be subject to
seizure, libel, and forfeiture.” 18 U.S.C. § 3669 . Congress deliberately broadened th is provision—it was
originally limited to “[a]utomobiles or any other vehicles” but later expanded to “any conveyance” to eliminate ambiguity about its scope.  See 18 U.S.C. § 3669
(Historical and Revision Notes) . And, similar to the
Alaska regime,  Section 1161 makes the federal seizure law  turn on the choices of the relevant sovereigns: Section 3669 does not apply where the alcohol
transaction complies with both State law and a duly
adopted and federally certified tribal ordinance . 18
U.S.C. § 1161.
Tribal governments have made similar judgments.
The Metlakatla Indian Community’s federally published Alcohol Possession Code declares as contraband any “airplane, boat, including fishing vessels,
motor vehicle, or thing of any kind whatsoever” used
in connection with violating its Law and Order Code.
73 Fed. Reg. 47,210, 47,212 (Aug. 13, 2008) . The Red

31





Lake Band of Chippewa Indians  likewise confiscated
an aircraft after a nonmember pilot landed on Lower
Red Lake and began fishing there unlawfully. Tom
Robertson, Red Lake Tribe Faces Water Rights Challenge, MPR News (Aug. 23, 2006) .4 The Band’s chairman later explained that such confiscations were intended to deter others from encroaching on tribal waters. Id. Hualapai Indian Tribe similarly confiscated a
powered paraglider following a flight over reservation
land the Tribe treated as unauthorized. Janice Wood,
Hualapai “Trespass” Pilot Reluctantly Enters Plea ,
General Aviation News (Mar. 16, 2009) . The pilot
later resolved the case by admitting to trespass and
endangerment and paying a fine. Id.
Those examples do not prove that every jurisdiction would punish Jouppi as Alaska did.  But they do
not need to.  Solem does not require uniformity. The
examples instead show something more modest: treating an aircraft used to commit or facilitate a local offense as integral to that offense is not the constitutional anomaly that Jouppi claims.
Here, the connection between means and gravity
is especially direct. Beaver is outside Alaska’s interconnected road system and aircraft are a principal
means of reaching it. Jouppi’s plane was therefore not
merely where the prohibited alcohol happened to be
located. It was the means by which Jouppi could overcome a geographic barrier  and carry alcohol into a
community that had affirmatively voted to exclude

4 The pilot  recovered his plane  after six weeks of negotiations, $4,000 in fines, and $2,000 in legal fees . See Associated
Press, Red Lake in a Remote Area of Northern Minnesota , Minnesota Public Radio (Mar. 21, 2005).

32





it—the community’s effort to protect against alcohol’s
well-known harms . In assessing the gravity of
Jouppi’s offense, the individualized inquiry requires
attention to context. Jouppi demands its erasure.
